overview.bigIdea: Data is information – facts, numbers and observations. The skill is to **collect → organise → present → read** it so that anyone can understand it at a glance.

ladder.a: Pictograph (with key) or bar graph (with scale)

overview.languagesTitle: Three ways to show the same data

languages.name: Table
languages.text: Tally marks and frequencies – exact counts.

languages.name: Pictograph
languages.text: Pictures with a key (1 picture = 5 students).

languages.name: Bar graph
languages.text: Bars of equal width; length shows value using a scale.

plan.text: Lesson 1: make one tally table from a list of 20 marks (a 3-mark question).
Lesson 2: read and draw a pictograph with a key, including half symbols.
Lessons 3–4: read bar graphs, then draw one on graph paper with a scale.
Check knowledge quiz; revisit after 1, 3, 7 days.

lessons.title: Collecting and organising data
lessons.hook: Your teacher asks 30 students their favourite sweet. A messy list of 30 answers tells you nothing at a glance – but a table with **tally marks** instantly shows which sweet wins.

core.def: Facts, numbers, measures, observations and other descriptions that convey information.
One line per item; every 5th line is drawn **across** the previous four to make a bundle of 5.
The number of times a value occurs (the count).
A table with the values, tally marks and frequencies.

explain: Go through the list **once**, making a tally mark for each item – do not count each value separately, you may miss some.
Check: the total of all frequencies must equal the number of items in the list.

example.q: Marks of 20 students: 5, 8, 7, 5, 6, 8, 9, 5, 7, 10, 8, 5, 6, 7, 8, 5, 10, 7, 8, 5. Make a frequency table. (Model paper Q34 style)
steps: Tally while reading the list once: 5 → 6 marks, 6 → 2, 7 → 4, 8 → 5, 9 → 1, 10 → 2.

mistakes: Drawing the 5th tally as a separate line instead of across the four.
Not checking that the frequencies add up to the total.
lessons.tip: Always write the check ‘Total = …’ under your table – it shows the examiner you verified your counts.
examAsk: Make a tally/frequency table from raw data.
Which value has the highest frequency?

cards.a: How many times a value occurs.

diagram.caption: Tally for 13: two bundles of 5 and 3 more.

lessons.title: Pictographs
lessons.hook: Instead of numbers, draw pictures! A **pictograph** uses symbols – but each symbol can stand for more than one thing. The **key** is the secret code you must read first.

core.def: Shows data using pictures or symbols.
Says what one symbol stands for, e.g. one book symbol = 2 books. It **must** be given.
Half a symbol = half the key value (key 4 → half = 2).
Value ÷ key = number of symbols to draw.

explain: Choose a key that divides the values nicely so you don’t need awkward parts of symbols.
Always give a title, category names and the key.

example.q: Key: 1 symbol = 5 students. The Mathematics Club has 5 symbols, Sports Club 7, Art Club 3. (a) Students in the Mathematics Club? (b) Which club is largest? (Model paper Q30)
steps: (b) Sports Club has the most symbols (7) → 35 students.

mistakes: Counting symbols but forgetting to multiply by the key.
Drawing a pictograph without a key.
lessons.tip: Write the calculation next to each row (5 × 5 = 25) – it earns method marks.
lessons.memory: Symbols × key = value. Value ÷ key = symbols.
examAsk: Draw a pictograph with a given key (Model paper Q32: 1 symbol = 2 books).

lessons.title: Reading bar graphs
lessons.hook: Drawing 500 little pictures is tiring. A **bar graph** replaces pictures with bars – the longer the bar, the bigger the value. With a good scale it can show even very large numbers.

core.def: Bars of **uniform width** with equal gaps; the length/height shows the value.
Tells what one unit of length stands for (1 unit = 4 saplings).
Read the top of the bar against the axis; compare lengths to find most/least.

explain: Before answering, read the **title, axis labels and scale** – they tell you what the bars mean.
Difference = subtract the two values; total = add all values.

example.q: A bar graph shows saplings planted: VI A 12, VI B 16, VI C 20, VI D 24, VI E 20. Which class planted the most? How many more than VI A?

mistakes: Reading the bar against the wrong gridline.
Ignoring the scale (counting units instead of values).
Adding instead of subtracting for ‘how many more’.
lessons.tip: Put a ruler across from the top of the bar to the axis to read the value exactly.

cards.q: Bars in a bar graph have…
The length of a bar shows…

diagram.title: Saplings planted by class
diagram.caption: Model paper Q28 data with scale 1 unit = 4 saplings.

lessons.title: Drawing bar graphs and choosing a scale
lessons.hook: A good graph is **accurate, clear and pleasing to look at**. The single most important choice is the **scale** – too small and bars run off the page, too big and they are too short to compare.

core.def: 1) Draw and label the axes. 2) Choose a scale. 3) Mark values on the axis. 4) Draw bars of equal width with equal gaps. 5) Title.
Pick a number that divides the values neatly and keeps the tallest bar on the page (values 12–24 → 1 unit = 4).
Always write it, e.g. ‘Scale: 1 unit = 4 saplings’.
Neat labels, sensible colours and a clear title make the graph effective.

explain: Divide each value by the scale to get the bar length: 20 ÷ 4 = 5 units.
Start the value axis at 0 – starting elsewhere makes differences look bigger than they are.

example.q: Draw a bar graph for saplings: VI A 12, VI B 16, VI C 20, VI D 24, VI E 20. (Model paper Q28, 3 marks)
steps: Scale: all values are multiples of 4 → 1 unit = 4 saplings.
Label axes (Class, Number of saplings), draw equal-width bars with equal gaps, write the title and scale.
example.answer: Bars of 3, 4, 5, 6 and 5 units with scale 1 unit = 4.

lessons.tip: Marks in a graph question are for: title, labelled axes, scale, correct bar heights, equal widths. Tick each one before moving on.
examAsk: Draw a bar graph with a suitable scale.
Choose a scale for given data.
Why must a scale be written?

formulas.name: Tally
formulas.f: bundle of 5 = four lines + one across

revision: Data = facts, numbers, measures, observations that give information.
Tally marks: bundle every 5; frequency = count of each value; frequencies add to the total.
Pictograph: pictures with a key; value = symbols × key; half symbol = half the key.
Every pictograph and bar graph needs a key/scale.
Bar graph: equal widths, equal gaps; length shows value; bars may be vertical or horizontal.
Choose a scale that divides the values neatly and fits the page; start the axis at 0.
Bar length = value ÷ scale; value = length × scale.
Read title, axes and scale before answering questions on a graph.

paper.what: MCQs: bar graph; bars can be horizontal
Draw a bar graph (scale 1 unit = 4 saplings)

sections.title: Drawing a graph · marks checklist
items: Bars or symbols of the correct size, equal widths and gaps.

sections.title: Reading a graph
items: Read the key or scale first.
Write the calculation for each value (symbols × key).

sections.title: Answer writing
items: Write the rule or definition in one line first, then apply it – rule lines earn marks even if the arithmetic slips.
Show every step on its own line (for example each division in a prime factorisation or each Kaprekar round).
Underline or box the final answer and write the unit (°, students, books) where there is one.
For ‘Give reason / Justify’ questions: state the rule, then show that the number or figure fits (or does not fit) it.

checklist: I can make a tally and frequency table from raw data.
I can read a pictograph using its key, including half symbols.
I can draw a pictograph with a given key.
I can read values, differences and totals from a bar graph.
I can choose a suitable scale and draw a bar graph with all labels.

method: Built on proven learning methods: see it as a picture first, understand why it works, learn from worked examples, then test yourself (active recall) and revisit after 1, 3 and 7 days (spaced revision).
